data.turoyo: Məd našifo, hayo ste kəmḥafḏ̣ila, kmaḥtila ʕal ḥḏoḏe, kəmmi, lašan d duʕṯo, d nofəq u səkkar diḏa mena. <...>
data.translation: Wenn sie getrocknet ist, heben sie sie auf. Sie legen (die Stücke) aufeinander, damit sie schwitzen und ihr Zucker austritt. <...>

rationale: Thin Infectum cell; inanimate food and explicit sugar emergence, without inventing a physical mechanism.

summary: example for sense 1 in Preterit Intransitive (JTM 1.1/58)

data.turoyo: <...> Bəṯr məd daʕiṯo, kfayšo tloṯ-arbʕo yawme taqriban, bəṯr kmawfəqila naqla ḥreto li šəmšo, kmanšəfila w hedi ktulalla w kəzza.
data.translation: <...> Nachdem (die ḥărire) geschwitzt hat, bleibt sie zwei, drei Tage so, dann bringen sie sie nochmals hinaus in die Sonne, trocknen sie, und dann heben sie sie auf, und dann ist sie fertig.

rationale: Thin Preterit Intransitive cell; completed sweating stage contrasts Infectum purpose in the same verse.

data.turoyo: W maḥtinawo orti naḏ̣ifo ʕal feme di qošxane, w bəṯr u qapaġ, ʕašan d, i naqqa d duḥṯo, d lə noḥət i daḥṯayo li rezo, huyowa ḥapṯo ḥapṯo, kuyo hawxa d saymət i rezo.
data.translation: Wir legten ein sauberes Tuch über die Öffnung des Kochtopfs, und danach den Deckel, damit, wenn der Reis schwitzt, dieses Kondenswasser nicht auf den Reis herabtropft. Er wurde körnig. Er wird (körnig), wenn du den Reis so machst.

rationale: Thin Infectum cell; cooking/condensation context is a participant extension rather than a new technical sense.

summary: example for sense 1 in Infectum (Lahdo The ḥalile/7)

data.turoyo: <...> gmaḥtila xud mәn, xud sanduqe d howe, b naylon w b sanduqe w gәmkasәlla, gdәḥso. <...>
data.translation: <...> They put it in things such as boxes, in plastic and boxes and they cover it. It sweats. <...>

rationale: Unusual local gdәḥso form and covered stored-food context; source s preserved.

summary: example for sense 1 in Infectum (MAC NI Three kinds of death/15)

data.translation: <...> The man, his sweat is pouring down his face, he is sweating. <...>
data.ref: MAC NI Three kinds of death/15

rationale: Thin Infectum cell; overt human subject and bodily sweat, brings cell to five.

data.turoyo: bəṯər me d daʕəṯina, əno saləqno lu bayto, <...>
data.translation: After we had sweated, I went up home, <...>

rationale: Thin Preterit Intransitive sense-1 cell after two cumulative examples; first-person plural bodily sweating, with explicit cut before further dialogue.

summary: The existing bodily sense covers both sweating and a sweaty state. Food subjects in JTM 1.1/58, JTM 2.8/4 and Lahdo The ḥalile/7 extend participant type; no separate technical meaning has been established.

JTM 1.1/58 contrasts purpose Infectum duʕṯo with completed Preterit Intransitive daʕiṯo. The latter’s feminine finite form is homographic with the masculine state Part act. at 29/78; clause structure and discourse determine the filing.
The root appears with ʕṯ and ḥṯ spellings, while Lahdo prints gdәḥso. Preserve every source form; the corpus does not license deriving a precise local sound rule from the German/English translation.

MAC NI Three kinds of death/15 distinguishes sweat as subject of the preceding flowing clause from the man as subject of kodoʕaṯ. The treatment purpose at 112/166 is another human bodily use, with no independent causative or Detransitive evidence.
JTM 1.1/58 has a Turoyo tloṯ-arbʕo versus German zwei, drei day-count difference. Both supplied texts are retained; it is unrelated to the verb’s meaning.
daʕəṯina is first-person plural Preterit Intransitive in a temporal after-clause. English had sweated expresses relative time; the source has no -wa and does not establish Preterit-wa.
The third Preterit Intransitive example after round 1 contributes a personal plural form and clear physical-exertion context. No Detransitive, causative or fixed collocation is present.
At JTM 2.8/4, is the feminine subject rice, the pot or its contents, and does duḥṯo name emitted moisture or a resulting wet surface? One attestation does not establish a separate culinary lexeme.
Confirm gdәḥso in Lahdo The ḥalile/7 and whether the product’s sweating refers to moisture, sugar coating or another process; no chemical explanation is inferred.
Check the day-count difference in JTM 1.1/58 against the edition; no silent translation correction is made.
Confirm the exact person-ending segmentation of daʕəṯina. Added English is the supplied project machine translation.
Inanimate confections and rice undergo a process described as sweating. Product moisture/sugar coating and lid condensation remain physical-process questions, not independent lexical senses.
Human exercise leads to sweating before going home/swimming; bodily meaning unchanged after the broader food-subject evidence of round 1.
